terms.comment: A description of ours: certāmen, contest, with the gerundive of fūnem trahere, pull a rope. We have found no Latin name for the game in Lewis & Short, Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini; the Greeks had one (see the alternative).

terms.gloss: play tug of war, by its Greek name
terms.grammar: helcystinda is an adverb, as in Greek, and does not decline
terms.comment: The Greek name of the game in Latin letters: ἑλκυστίνδα or διελκυστίνδα παίζειν, “play at pulling”, from ἕλκω, pull. Pollux has διελκυστίνδα (9.112; Liddell & Scott: tug-of-war), and Eustathius ἑλκυστίνδα (1111.24). We have found no Latin author who uses the name, so the Latin spelling is ours.

phrases.latin: Utra pars plūs valet? Fūne certēmus.
phrases.english: Which side is stronger? Let’s have a tug of war.

sources: Lewis & Short: certamen · Lewis & Short: funis · Lewis & Short: traho
Liddell & Scott: διελκυστίνδα · Liddell & Scott: ἑλκυστίνδα
